title: Milk for a Hangover: Does It Help? Plus Chocolate Milk
excerpt: Does milk help a hangover? What the hydration research says about milk and chocolate milk, why milk doesn't really coat your stomach, and when it makes nausea or heartburn worse.
metaDescription: Does milk help a hangover? What milk and chocolate milk can and can't do, the 'coats your stomach' myth, and when milk makes nausea worse.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** milk can help a hangover a little, but not for the reasons most people think. A glass of cold milk is a decent way to get fluid, some electrolytes, protein and a bit of sugar into a body that's running low on all four, and research on hydration suggests milk stays in the body longer than plain water does. What milk does *not* do is "coat your stomach," neutralize alcohol, or fix the headache, fatigue and foggy mood that make up most of a hangover. For some people with a queasy stomach, milk actually makes things worse. Chocolate milk is a reasonable variation if you can keep it down, mostly because of the extra carbohydrate.

**The quick rules:** If milk sounds good and your stomach is settled, a glass of plain or chocolate milk is a fine part of a hangover breakfast. If you feel nauseous, have heartburn, or are lactose intolerant, start with small sips of water or an electrolyte drink instead and save milk for later. Don't rely on a glass of milk before going out to "line your stomach." A real meal does that job far better. And no drink, milk included, makes up for how much you drank.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover gets steadily better over the day. **Call 911 or get emergency care if** someone is confused, can't be woken, is having a seizure, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue-tinged or very pale skin, or keeps vomiting while drowsy. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. **See a doctor soon if** you can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, you see blood in your vomit or black, tarry stools, you have severe or worsening belly pain, or you feel dizzy or faint when you stand. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart or anxiety when you stop or cut back, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than trying to ride it out.

## Why a Drink Can Only Do So Much for a Hangover

It helps to know what you're up against. A hangover isn't one problem. It's several things happening at once:

- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol blocks a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more than you drink. That's where the dry mouth and thirst come from.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, so you wake up tired even after eight hours in bed.
- **Inflammation.** Researchers have found that hangovers are linked to an immune-style response, the same kind of chemical signals your body releases when you're fighting off a cold. That partly explains the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product, before breaking it down further. It's thought to contribute to nausea, flushing and feeling unwell.
- **Low blood sugar and an irritated stomach.** Alcohol can drop blood sugar a bit and irritates the stomach lining, which adds shakiness and nausea.

Here's the part that surprises people: studies that measured hangover severity against blood markers of hydration and electrolytes have found only a weak link between them. Dehydration makes you feel worse, but it isn't the main driver of a hangover. That's why chugging water, sports drinks or milk takes the edge off thirst and dizziness without making the hangover go away.

So the fair question isn't "does milk cure a hangover?" Nothing does. It's "is milk a good thing to drink while your body recovers?" The answer to that is more interesting.

## What Milk Actually Brings to the Table

A cup (about 240 ml) of cow's milk is mostly water, plus a useful mix of other things. Roughly, depending on the fat level:

| Component | About how much per cup | Why it matters after drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Water | Around 88-90% of the volume | Replaces fluid you lost overnight |
| Protein | About 8 g | Slows how fast the fluid leaves your stomach and helps you feel fuller |
| Carbohydrate (lactose) | About 12 g | A little sugar if your blood sugar is low |
| Sodium | About 100 mg | Helps your body hold on to the fluid you drink |
| Potassium | About 350-400 mg | Another electrolyte you lose through urine |
| Calcium | About 300 mg | Good for you, but not a hangover factor |
| Fat | 0 to 8 g, depending on type | Slows stomach emptying; can be hard on a queasy stomach |

None of these is unusual on its own. What's interesting is the combination: fluid plus sodium plus protein plus some sugar is close to what sports scientists recommend for rehydrating after hard exercise.

### The hydration research

The best evidence for milk as a hydrating drink doesn't come from hangover studies. It comes from exercise and hydration research.

- A study led by Susan Shirreffs and Ron Maughan, published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* in 2007, had people dehydrate through exercise and then rehydrate with different drinks. Skimmed milk, including a version with added sodium, was retained by the body better than water or a standard sports drink over the following hours. In other words, people urinated less of it back out.
- A larger 2016 study by Maughan and colleagues in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* created a "beverage hydration index," which compares how much of a drink is still in your body two hours later versus the same amount of water. Both skimmed and full-fat milk scored among the highest of the 13 drinks tested, alongside an oral rehydration solution and ahead of plain water, sports drinks, cola, coffee and beer.

The likely reasons are the sodium and potassium (which help your body keep water instead of passing it) and the protein and fat (which slow how fast the drink empties from your stomach, so the fluid trickles into your system instead of rushing through).

**What this does and doesn't tell us.** These studies were done on healthy people who were mildly dehydrated from exercise or who simply drank the test beverages, not on people with a hangover. It's a reasonable guess that milk would rehydrate you well the morning after drinking too, but there is no good evidence from trials that milk reduces hangover symptoms specifically. Treat it as a good fluid, not a remedy.

## So, Does Milk Help a Hangover?

Here's a fair breakdown of where milk earns its place and where it doesn't.

**Where milk can genuinely help:**

- **Rehydration that lasts.** If your stomach is settled, milk is one of the better everyday drinks for getting fluid back into your body and keeping it there.
- **A gentle bit of fuel.** Many people can't face food on a hangover morning. A glass of milk gives you some protein and sugar without having to chew anything, which can steady you enough to eat a proper meal later.
- **Comfort.** Cold milk is soothing for a lot of people, and feeling slightly better is worth something when you're miserable.

**Where milk doesn't help, or can backfire:**

- **It doesn't treat the headache, fatigue or brain fog.** Those come from poor sleep, inflammation and the after-effects of alcohol on your brain, and milk doesn't touch them.
- **It doesn't speed up how fast alcohol leaves your body.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace. No drink speeds that up in a meaningful way.
- **It can make nausea worse.** Fat and protein slow down how fast your stomach empties. That's good for hydration when you feel fine, but if you're already queasy, a heavy, full-fat drink sitting in your stomach can push you toward vomiting.
- **It can trigger heartburn.** More on this below.
- **It's a problem if you're lactose intolerant.** Alcohol already irritates the gut, and lactose can add bloating, cramps and diarrhea on top.

If you're nauseous, it's usually smarter to start with small sips of water, an electrolyte drink or [coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover), and bring milk in once your stomach has calmed down. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers that first hour in more detail.

## The "Milk Coats Your Stomach" Myth

This is the most common reason people reach for milk, either before drinking or the morning after. The idea is that milk forms a protective layer over your stomach lining. It doesn't, at least not in any lasting way.

Milk is a liquid, and it moves through the stomach and gets broken down like any other food. Any soothing feeling you get is short-lived. The history here is useful: for much of the 20th century, doctors treated stomach ulcers with a milk-heavy diet (often called the Sippy diet) on the theory that milk would protect the stomach. That approach was dropped once research showed that milk briefly buffers stomach acid but then stimulates the stomach to make *more* acid, largely because of its protein and calcium. Today, ulcer guidance doesn't recommend milk as a treatment.

What that means for you:

- **After drinking**, a glass of milk might feel soothing for a few minutes, but it isn't protecting your stomach lining and can make acid symptoms worse an hour later.
- **Before drinking**, milk does slow things down a bit, but only because it's food in your stomach. It isn't a shield.

## Milk and Heartburn After Drinking

Alcohol relaxes the ring of muscle at the bottom of your esophagus that normally keeps stomach acid where it belongs. That's why a big night can leave you with burning in your chest or a sour taste the next morning.

Milk is a classic home remedy for heartburn, and it can bring brief relief as it washes acid down and buffers it. But for the reasons above, it can also lead to a rebound. Full-fat milk is the bigger culprit, because fat also relaxes that same muscle and keeps food in your stomach longer.

If heartburn is your main symptom, a small amount of skimmed milk is less likely to cause trouble than a big glass of whole milk, but an over-the-counter antacid is a more reliable fix. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) walks through what actually helps and when frequent heartburn is worth mentioning to a doctor.

## Chocolate Milk for a Hangover

Chocolate milk has a reputation as a recovery drink, mostly thanks to athletes. Is it any better than plain milk the morning after?

**What's different about it.** Chocolate milk has the same water, protein and electrolytes as regular milk, plus extra sugar. A typical store-bought cup has roughly twice the carbohydrate of plain milk, with a mix of lactose and added sugar. It also has a little cocoa, which contains a small amount of caffeine and a related compound called theobromine, though the amounts in a glass are much lower than in a cup of coffee.

**Where the "recovery drink" reputation comes from.** A small 2006 study by Jason Karp and colleagues in the *International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism* found that trained cyclists who drank low-fat chocolate milk between hard workouts performed as well as or better in a second session than when they drank a commercial carbohydrate sports drink. Several later studies have looked at chocolate milk after exercise with broadly similar, though mixed, results. The thinking is that the carbohydrate-to-protein mix helps refuel muscles.

**How that applies to a hangover.** Again, a hangover isn't a workout. You haven't drained your muscle fuel, so the "refueling" benefit doesn't really carry over. What does carry over:

- **The extra sugar can help if you're shaky or lightheaded** and haven't eaten. Alcohol can lower blood sugar a bit, and a sweet drink can take the edge off that.
- **It's easier to get down.** Some people find chocolate milk more appealing than plain milk or food when they feel rough.
- **The small dose of caffeine** may help a little if you're a regular coffee drinker and are getting a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of your hangover. Don't count on it, though. The amount is small.

**The downsides** are the same as plain milk, plus more sugar. If your stomach is unsettled, a thick, sweet, dairy drink is often the last thing it wants. And if you drink a lot of sugary drinks, the added sugar adds up.

**Verdict:** chocolate milk is a fine choice if it sounds good and your stomach can handle it. It's not a hangover cure, and there is no good evidence that it works better than plain milk, water with a light breakfast, or an electrolyte drink. Low-fat chocolate milk is usually gentler than whole.

## Drinking Milk Before Alcohol: Does It "Line Your Stomach"?

A glass of milk before a night out is an old tip, especially in the UK and Ireland. Here's what's true and what isn't.

**What's true.** Having food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood. Alcohol is absorbed mostly in the small intestine, and food keeps it in the stomach longer, where some of it is broken down before it's ever absorbed. Studies comparing drinking on an empty stomach versus after a meal have found noticeably lower peak blood alcohol levels after eating. Milk contains protein and fat, so it counts as food and will slow absorption a little.

**What isn't true.** A single glass of milk is a small amount of food. It won't slow absorption nearly as much as a proper meal with protein, fat and fiber. It doesn't form a protective barrier, and it doesn't change how much alcohol eventually reaches your bloodstream if you keep drinking. It just shifts the timing. There is no good evidence that a glass of milk before drinking prevents a hangover.

**What works better.** Eat a real meal before you start, such as something with protein, healthy fats and complex carbohydrates. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the best options, and [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains exactly why skipping that meal hits so hard. If a glass of milk is all you can manage before you go, it's better than nothing. Just don't treat it as protection.

## Mixing Milk and Alcohol in the Same Drink

Creamy drinks such as White Russians, mudslides, eggnog and Irish cream liqueurs mix dairy with alcohol. A few points worth knowing:

- **The dairy doesn't cancel out the alcohol.** It may slow absorption slightly, the way any food does, but these drinks are often strong and easy to drink quickly because the cream hides the taste of the alcohol.
- **They're heavy on fat and sugar,** which can make next-morning nausea and heartburn worse for some people.
- **Milk curdles with acid.** Mixing milk or cream with citrus juice or acidic mixers causes clumping. It isn't dangerous, but it's unpleasant, and some people find it upsets their stomach.
- **Lactose intolerance doesn't go away when you're drinking.** If dairy normally bothers you, a few cream liqueurs can leave you with a rough gut the next day that has nothing to do with the alcohol itself.

## Lactose Intolerance, Alcohol and Your Gut

Many adults digest lactose poorly, and it's especially common in people of East Asian, African, Hispanic and Indigenous American descent. If that's you, milk after drinking is a double hit. Alcohol irritates the gut and speeds things through, and undigested lactose pulls water into the intestine and feeds gas-producing bacteria. The result can be cramps, bloating and diarrhea.

If you get [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) and you also had milk, the milk may be part of the story. Lactose-free milk is a good swap. It has the same protein, electrolytes and fluid without the lactose, so you keep the hydration benefits. Soy milk is another option with a similar protein content, though it hasn't been studied for hydration the way cow's milk has. Most other plant milks (almond, oat, rice) are much lower in protein and don't have the same profile, so think of them as tasty fluids rather than a match for dairy.

## Milk vs. Other Hangover Drinks

Here's how milk stacks up against the other things people reach for on a hangover morning.

| Drink | Main strengths | Main drawbacks | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water | Gentle, free, easy on a queasy stomach | Passes through faster; no electrolytes or fuel | First thing, especially if nauseous |
| Plain milk | Retained well, protein, some electrolytes and sugar | Can worsen nausea or heartburn; lactose issues | Settled stomach, can't face food yet |
| Chocolate milk | Same as milk plus extra carbohydrate | More sugar; heavy if you feel sick | Shaky, low on fuel, settled stomach |
| Oral rehydration drinks (e.g. Pedialyte) | Designed for rehydration, gentle | Cost; not tasty for everyone | Lots of fluid loss, vomiting or diarrhea |
| Sports drinks | Some sodium and sugar, widely available | Lower sodium than rehydration drinks; sugary | Mild dehydration |
| Coconut water | High in potassium, light | Low in sodium | Light rehydration |
| Coffee | Helps with caffeine-withdrawal headaches | Can irritate stomach; slightly increases urination | Regular coffee drinkers, after some water |

For a closer look at the electrolyte options, see [Pedialyte vs. Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) and our full roundup of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

A sensible order on a rough morning: small sips of water or an electrolyte drink first, then milk or chocolate milk once your stomach can take it, then a real meal.

## What About Yogurt, Kefir and Other Dairy?

Several cultures have a dairy-based hangover tradition, like the salty yogurt drink ayran in Turkey or a glass of buttermilk or lassi in South Asia. These make some sense: they're fluid, they often contain salt, and fermented dairy tends to be easier on the gut for people who handle lactose poorly, because the bacteria have already broken some of it down.

There is no good evidence that yogurt, kefir or fermented dairy treats a hangover. But as part of a gentle breakfast, plain yogurt is a reasonable choice: it's soft, easy to eat, and has protein. Pair it with fruit such as a banana for potassium, or with toast. [Eggs](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) are another easy protein many people tolerate well the morning after.

## Milk Thistle Is Not Milk

People searching for "milk for a hangover" sometimes land on milk thistle, so it's worth clearing up. Milk thistle is a plant. Its extract, silymarin, is sold as a liver-support supplement. It has nothing to do with dairy, and drinking milk gives you none of it. The research on milk thistle for liver health is mixed, and there is no good evidence that it treats hangovers. If you're curious how it compares with other liver-focused supplements, see our [DHM vs. milk thistle comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-milk-thistle-which-liver-supplement-more-effective-2025).

## How to Use Milk on a Hangover Morning

If you want to try milk, here's a practical way to do it without upsetting your stomach.

1. **Start with water.** A glass of water or an electrolyte drink, sipped slowly, gives your stomach a chance to settle.
2. **Check in with your stomach.** If you're nauseous or have heartburn, wait. Milk will still be there in an hour.
3. **Go small and cold.** Half a glass of cold milk is easier to handle than a big glass. Skimmed or low-fat milk is gentler than whole.
4. **Try chocolate milk if you're shaky.** The extra sugar may help if you haven't eaten anything.
5. **Follow it with real food.** Milk works best as a bridge to breakfast, not a replacement for it. Toast, eggs, oatmeal, a banana or plain yogurt are all good choices.
6. **Keep drinking fluids through the day.** Milk can be one of them, but water should be most of it.
7. **Skip it if dairy doesn't agree with you.** Use lactose-free milk or stick to other drinks.

## The Bigger Picture: Preventing the Next One

Milk is a fine thing to drink while you recover. But if you find yourself looking up hangover remedies often, the drink you have the morning after matters much less than what happens the night before. The habits with the best evidence are dull but effective: eat a proper meal before drinking, pace yourself (roughly one drink an hour or slower), alternate alcoholic drinks with water, choose clearer drinks over dark ones, and get as much sleep as you can. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each one.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with only limited human data, so it's promising but not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace eating, pacing and hydrating. If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Milk is a good rehydrating drink. Hydration research suggests the body keeps more of it than plain water, thanks to its electrolytes, protein and fat.
- It can help you feel a bit better on a hangover morning, especially if you can't face food yet, but it doesn't treat the headache, fatigue or brain fog, and it doesn't speed up how fast alcohol leaves your body.
- Milk doesn't coat or protect your stomach. It can make nausea and heartburn worse, especially full-fat milk.
- Chocolate milk adds carbohydrate, which may help if you're shaky, but there's no good evidence it beats plain milk or water plus breakfast.
- A glass of milk before drinking is a weak substitute for a real meal.
- If you're lactose intolerant, use lactose-free milk or skip dairy.
- If you can't keep fluids down, or you notice signs of alcohol poisoning or withdrawal, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does milk help a hangover?**

A little. Milk is a good rehydrating drink because its sodium, potassium, protein and fat help your body hold on to the fluid, and it gives you some protein and sugar if you can't face food yet. It doesn't treat the headache, fatigue or brain fog, and it doesn't speed up how fast alcohol leaves your body. If your stomach is upset, start with water or an electrolyte drink and try milk later.

**Is chocolate milk good for a hangover?**

It can be a reasonable choice if your stomach is settled. Chocolate milk has the same fluid, protein and electrolytes as plain milk plus extra carbohydrate, which may help if you feel shaky or haven't eaten. Its reputation comes from exercise recovery studies, not hangover research, and there is no good evidence that it works better than plain milk or water with a light breakfast. Low-fat versions are usually easier on the stomach.

**Does drinking milk before alcohol line your stomach?**

Not in the way people think. Milk doesn't form a protective coating. Because it contains protein and fat, it counts as a small amount of food and can slow alcohol absorption slightly, but a single glass does far less than a proper meal. There is no good evidence that a glass of milk before drinking prevents a hangover. Eating a real meal before you start is much more effective.

**Can milk make a hangover worse?**

For some people, yes. Fat and protein slow how fast your stomach empties, which can make nausea worse if you're already queasy. Milk can also cause rebound heartburn because it stimulates stomach acid after briefly buffering it. If you're lactose intolerant, it can add cramps, bloating and diarrhea on top of an alcohol-irritated gut.

**Is milk better than water for a hangover?**

Milk tends to stay in your body longer than water. A 2016 study that compared 13 common drinks found that both skimmed and full-fat milk were retained better than plain water over the following hours. But water is gentler on a nauseous stomach, so the best approach is usually water or an electrolyte drink first, then milk once your stomach has settled.

**Does milk help with heartburn after drinking?**

Only briefly. Milk can wash acid down and soothe the burning for a few minutes, but its protein and calcium then prompt the stomach to make more acid, and full-fat milk can relax the muscle that keeps acid out of your esophagus. A small amount of skimmed milk is less likely to backfire, but an over-the-counter antacid is a more reliable option.

**Is milk thistle the same as drinking milk for a hangover?**

No. Milk thistle is a plant whose extract, silymarin, is sold as a liver-support supplement. It has nothing to do with dairy. The research on milk thistle for liver health is mixed, and there is no good evidence that it treats hangovers.
